title: 1 Chronicles 3:1–9
context: Chapter 3 turns to the sons of David and so to the royal line itself. Verses 1–4 list six sons born in Hebron, with their mothers, and they note that David reigned there seven years and six months, and thirty-three years in Jerusalem, a length also given in 2 Samuel 5:4–5. The Hebron list parallels 2 Samuel 3:2–5. The names and births are close, but they are not identical: the second son is Daniel, of Abigail the Carmelitess, here, whereas 2 Samuel 3:3 calls him Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. The difference should be named, not explained away. Verses 5–8 then list sons born in Jerusalem, four by Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel—Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon—and nine more, ending with a second Elishama and a second Eliphelet, and including Nogah, who does not appear in 2 Samuel 5:14–16. That Samuel list has Shammua rather than Shimea, Elishua rather than the first Elishama of 3:6, and eleven names rather than the thirteen counted here as four plus nine. 2 Samuel 11 also names Solomon’s mother Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, a naming that differs from Bathshua, daughter of Ammiel, in 3:5. Another list of David’s Jerusalem sons stands later in this book, at 1 Chronicles 14:4–7. The already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15 record that the Chronicles parallels differ in some names and that both traditions treat the lists as historical record and do not build doctrine on the variations. That restraint should be kept here. Verse 9 adds the sons of the concubines, unnamed, and Tamar their sister. Both traditions read the unit as the Chronicler tracing David’s house, the royal line already in view since 2:15, without allegory and without a forced harmony of the counts and spellings.

verses.text: Now these were the sons of David, who were born to him in Hebron: the firstborn, Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; the second, Daniel, of Abigail the Carmelitess;
verses.arminianNotes:
The sons born in Hebron begin: the firstborn Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and the second, Daniel, of Abigail the Carmelitess. 2 Samuel 3:2–3 has Amnon of Ahinoam, then Chileab of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. The second son’s name differs—Daniel here, Chileab there—and the description of Abigail is shorter here. The difference should be left standing.

Arminian readers take both lists as historical notices of the same household, not as a problem that must be solved by a theory the text does not give.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the 2 Samuel 3:2–5 parallel without harmonizing Daniel and Chileab. The Chronicler is opening David’s Hebron family, the first step of the royal line in this chapter.

Both traditions treat the lists as historical record, name the Samuel parallels without harmonizing the differences, and do not build doctrine on the variations, which matches the already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15.

verses.text: the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith;
verses.arminianNotes:
The third is Absalom, son of Maacah daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; the fourth is Adonijah, son of Haggith. These two match 2 Samuel 3:3–4, and the already drafted Samuel notes already point forward to Absalom’s later rebellion and Adonijah’s bid for the throne. This verse only names them, with their mothers.

Arminian readers keep the genealogical form. The later stories remain in Samuel and Kings; here the brothers stand in birth order.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same parallel. The royal household includes these sons, recorded without the narratives that will follow in the earlier books.

Both traditions treat the lists as historical record, name the Samuel parallels without harmonizing the differences, and do not build doctrine on the variations, which matches the already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15.

verses.text: the fifth, Shephatiah of Abital; the sixth, Ithream by Eglah his wife:
verses.arminianNotes:
The fifth is Shephatiah of Abital; the sixth is Ithream by Eglah his wife. The two complete the Hebron six and match 2 Samuel 3:4–5, with only small differences of phrasing. The list is still a record of births, not a ranking of future kings.

Arminian readers take Shephatiah and Ithream as historical sons, little narrated later, and still part of David’s house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stay with the 2 Samuel 3:4–5 parallel. Six sons of Hebron are now named, and the next verse will count them and date the two reigns.

Both traditions treat the lists as historical record, name the Samuel parallels without harmonizing the differences, and do not build doctrine on the variations, which matches the already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15.

verses.text: six were born to him in Hebron; and he reigned there seven years and six months. He reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem;
verses.arminianNotes:
“six were born to him in Hebron; and he reigned there seven years and six months. He reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem;” The count matches the six just listed. The two lengths of reign agree with 2 Samuel 5:5, which also gives seven years and six months in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.

Arminian readers hear a straightforward historical summary, tying the Hebron family to the years of the Hebron reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same agreement with 2 Samuel 5:4–5 as a shared chronological notice, not a cue for allegory. The Jerusalem sons will now follow.

Both traditions treat the lists as historical record, name the Samuel parallels without harmonizing the differences, and do not build doctrine on the variations, which matches the already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15.

verses.text: and these were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon, four, by Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel;
verses.arminianNotes:
Four sons were born in Jerusalem to Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. 2 Samuel 5:14 has Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon, and does not name the mother in that verse. 2 Samuel 11 names Solomon’s mother Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, which differs from Bathshua, daughter of Ammiel, here. The names and the parentage should be reported as the lists give them, not forced into one form.

Arminian readers keep Nathan and Solomon side by side in the record, as 2 Samuel 5:14 already does, without a special mark on Solomon in this verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name those differences and, with the drafted 2 Samuel 5 notes, refuse to build doctrine on the variations. The four are the first Jerusalem sons in this chapter’s count.

Both traditions treat the lists as historical record, name the Samuel parallels without harmonizing the differences, and do not build doctrine on the variations, which matches the already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15.

verses.arminianNotes:
The Jerusalem list continues: “and Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet,” 2 Samuel 5:15 has Ibhar and then Elishua, not Elishama, before Nepheg and Japhia, which this chapter will reach in the next verse after Nogah. Elishama and Eliphelet will also appear again in verse 8. The differences of name and of repetition should be named, not erased.

Arminian readers take this verse as this book’s own form of the list, a historical register with its own wording.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise point to 2 Samuel 5:15 and to the double appearance of some names later in this list, without a required scheme that makes every form identical.

Both traditions treat the lists as historical record, name the Samuel parallels without harmonizing the differences, and do not build doctrine on the variations, which matches the already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15.

verses.arminianNotes:
“Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,” follow. Nepheg and Japhia stand in 2 Samuel 5:15; Nogah does not appear in that Samuel list. The extra name is a real difference of content, not only of spelling, and should be left as such.

Arminian readers will not drop Nogah to make the lists match, nor invent a reason the verse does not give for his absence from 2 Samuel 5.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report Nogah as part of this chapter’s Jerusalem sons, a difference from 2 Samuel 5:14–16 already acknowledged in the Samuel notes as a matter of the record, not of doctrine.

Both traditions treat the lists as historical record, name the Samuel parallels without harmonizing the differences, and do not build doctrine on the variations, which matches the already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15.

verses.arminianNotes:
The nine close with “Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine.” Eliada and Eliphelet stand at the end of 2 Samuel 5:16 as well, and Elishama also appears there; here Elishama and Eliphelet have already been named in verse 6. The count “nine” covers verses 6–8. Together with the four of verse 5, the chapter numbers thirteen sons in Jerusalem, where 2 Samuel 5:14–16 lists eleven names.

Arminian readers leave the two counts and the repeated names as differences between the records.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers do the same. The parallel is clear, the numbers and some names differ, and no party contrast is needed to explain that fact.

Both traditions treat the lists as historical record, name the Samuel parallels without harmonizing the differences, and do not build doctrine on the variations, which matches the already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15.

verses.text: All these were the sons of David, in addition to the sons of the concubines; and Tamar was their sister.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All these were the sons of David, in addition to the sons of the concubines; and Tamar was their sister.” The sons of the concubines are mentioned, not named. Tamar, their sister, is named, as she is known from 2 Samuel 13, though that story is not retold here.

Arminian readers take the close as a complete heading over David’s children so far as this unit goes: the named sons, other sons, and Tamar.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same summary. The royal house includes more children than the numbered lists, and Tamar is recorded as sister to these sons, without the later narrative being imported in full.

Both traditions treat the lists as historical record, name the Samuel parallels without harmonizing the differences, and do not build doctrine on the variations, which matches the already drafted notes on 2 Samuel 5:15.
